summary: China's factories shrank again in October as holiday spending faded and export orders fell, while AI-linked companies kept booming and AI stocks kept falling.
body: China's official manufacturing purchasing managers' index (PMI), a monthly survey of factory managers, fell to 49.3 in October from 50.1 in September, the National Bureau of Statistics said on Saturday [^1][^2]. A reading below 50 means activity is shrinking; economists polled by Reuters had expected 50.0 [^1]. It is the third contraction in four months, and a similar index for services and construction also slipped below 50, to 49.7 [^1][^2]. New orders fell, and export orders stayed weak [^1][^3].

The reasons given: Christmas export orders were placed early, in September; the spending boost from the early-October National Day holiday faded; and demand at home is weak [^1]. "Insufficient demand is increasing downward pressure on the economy," said Zhang Liqun of the government-linked China Federation of Logistics and Purchasing [^1]. China's economy grew 4.5% in the third quarter, at the bottom of this year's 4.5% to 5% target range [^2].

The picture is split. Makers of trains, ships, aircraft and electronics reported strong readings, and AI-linked firms are booming, while companies tied to housing struggle; furniture maker Oppein's profit fell 80% [^1]. Investors are cooling too: the STAR50 index of Chinese AI and chip stocks has fallen about 40% in under four months, wiping out about US$480 billion, Reuters reports [^4].

My read: for ordinary families, weak demand at home shows up as cautious spending and a hard job market, even as the country pours money into AI and chips. Whether Beijing adds more support, such as the mortgage subsidies some economists suggest, is the thing to watch [^1].
